name: Sponsorship

CREATORS.summary: The advertising agency stopped being a space broker and became a production company. Under sponsorship the network sold an hour of time and almost nothing else; the advertiser's agency wrote the show, hired the star, booked the orchestra, cleared the talent, and delivered a finished program to the line. The FCC said so in its own words in 1941: 'the network further delegates the actual production of programs to advertising agencies... it is frequently neither the station nor the network, but rather the advertising agency, which determines what broadcast programs shall contain.' J. Walter Thompson ran the biggest program factory (Kraft Music Hall, Lux Radio Theatre, the Chase and Sanborn Hour), with nine weekly network shows sponsored by its clients as early as 1933; Blackett-Sample-Hummert built the daytime serial line; Benton & Bowles, Young & Rubicam and BBDO each held signature properties. The pay for all of this was the same 15 percent commission on media that era 1 had settled around 1920 - the agency earned its cut on the time and threw the show in. That is the era's defining agency fact: the commission bought content production, so the marginal cost of a program to the advertiser looked like zero even though it was not. Agency scale grew with it - N.W. Ayer's gross receipts went from $13.7M in 1919 to $38.0M in 1930, and JWT's billings passed $37.5M by the end of the 1920s. Agencies also opened Hollywood offices, ran their own radio departments, and, through men like McCann-Erickson's Marion Harper and Hans Zeisel, did the research that killed the industry's own ratings service in 1946.

BUYERS.summary: The era's marginal new buyer class was the national packaged-goods advertiser who wanted a daily habit rather than a seasonal campaign - soap, coffee, cereal, cigarettes, drugs. Procter & Gamble is the archetype: it commissioned the daytime serial, which is why the form is called the soap opera, and its research director D.P. Smelser chaired the governing board of the industry's ratings service in the late 1930s, so the largest buyer of audience also chaired the body that counted it. Buyers came in four money types that behaved very differently. National brand money was the era's growth engine and it peaked, strikingly, during the war: national advertisers were 51.7 percent of all US ad dollars in 1935 and 61.3 percent in 1944-45, when the excess-profits tax made institutional advertising nearly free and there was often nothing to sell. Local retail money - department stores, grocers, auto dealers - stayed about two fifths of the total and was the base load of every newspaper. Classified money came from individuals and small firms buying by the line and is not separately reported anywhere before 1950. Direct-response money ran through the mail and was large all era. Buyers also shifted how they bought inside radio: network sponsorship took 55.8 percent of radio dollars in 1935 but only 35.6 percent by 1949, as national spot and local spot grew faster. And the buyers of audience data changed too - within four years of the CAB's 1930 launch, agency subscribers (27) outnumbered advertiser subscribers (17), which is the moment the agency became the market's real information buyer.

SELLERS.summary: Two kinds of seller mattered. Newspapers stayed the largest single owner of audience for every one of these thirty-two years, selling mostly to local retailers through the rate card that era 1 had made enforceable with audited circulation. The new seller was the radio network, and it was far more concentrated than print. The FCC's 1941 Report on Chain Broadcasting - the era's best audited numbers - found that in 1938 the whole US broadcast industry sold $100,892,259 of net time, of which the NBC and CBS networks took 44 percent and their twenty-three owned stations another 7 percent, so two companies handled more than half the industry's business. Mutual, a cooperative with no rate card of its own, took about 2 percent. Stations affiliated with NBC or CBS held over 85 percent of the country's nighttime wattage. The networks were also the era's dominant intermediary: they kept 73 percent of network net time sales and paid just 27 percent to the 253 affiliates who actually put the signal in the air, and their combined network and owned-station operating income was roughly half of the industry's total. Government broke the top of that structure: the FCC's chain-broadcasting rules forced RCA to sell NBC Blue, which Edward J. Noble bought in October 1943 for $8 million and renamed the American Broadcasting Company. Then the seller base exploded - about 900 AM stations in 1945 became roughly 2,500 by the early 1950s - which is what pulled radio dollars from network sponsorship toward spot.

MEDIUM.summary: The chart contradicts the chapter title, and that is the point. Newspapers were the largest US advertising medium in every single year from 1918 to 1949, never falling below 32 percent of all spend even at radio's peak; they ended the era at 36.7 percent. Direct mail was the number two named medium in every year the Coen series splits by medium, running 14 to 16.5 percent of all spend - which places the measured-response tradition in the 1920s and 1930s, not in the 1970s. Radio, the era's mechanism innovation, peaked at 14.9 percent of all US advertising in 1945 and never came close to print. Magazines ran 7 to 12 percent, business papers 3 to 7 percent, billboards under 3 percent, farm publications about 1 percent. The war rearranged the mix without changing the ranking: between 1942 and 1945 business-paper advertising grew 108 percent and magazines 92 percent while newspapers grew only 15 percent and direct mail actually fell, a pattern consistent with paper supply limits rather than lost demand. Two tracked categories cannot be separated in this era. Directories and Yellow Pages sit inside Coen's 'Miscellaneous' residual, which was 19.6 percent of 1949 spend and is not broken out until 1980, even though Bell had taken directory ad sales in-house in 1920 and registered the Yellow Pages trademark in 1948. Classified sits inside newspaper local. Television appears in the series for the first time in 1949 at $58 million, 1.1 percent of the market - the whole of era 3's story is still ahead.

SCALE.summary: US advertising spend went from $1,930 million in 1919 to $5,210 million in 1949 - a 2.7x nominal rise, about 3.4 percent a year, with the deepest peacetime collapse in the series in the middle. From the 1929 peak of $2,850 million the market fell 53.5 percent to $1,325 million in 1933 and did not clear its 1929 nominal level again until 1943. Measured against the economy the picture inverts the usual story: advertising's share of GDP hit 3.0 percent in 1922, the highest reading in the entire 1919-2007 Coen/BEA series, and fell almost continuously afterward to a wartime low of 1.2 percent in 1944 before recovering to 1.9 percent in 1949. Anyone arguing that a later era 'captured' an unprecedented share of the economy has to explain 1922 first. The money-type split at the era's end: national brand $2,234M, local retail $1,876M, classified about $340M, direct response (direct mail) $756M. Two honesty flags for the dataset layer. First, before 1935 there is no medium or national/local split at all, and the 1920s figures were revised down about 15 percent, so the first sixteen years of the signature chart are estimate-grade. Second, Coen's radio numbers run well above the FCC's audited figures for the same year - $167M against $100.9M of industry net time sales in 1938 - which is consistent with the McCann-Erickson series being built on list rate-card prices rather than transaction prices. No contemporaneous world survey exists for this era; the global figure below is triangulated, not found.

claims.statement: World advertising expenditure in 1949 was on the order of $7.5 billion, of which the United States was roughly 70 percent. No contemporaneous world survey exists for this era.
claims.unit: US$ billions of estimated world advertising expenditure, 1949
claims.method: Two paths. (a) Bottom-up: US spend $5.21B at 1.9 percent of GDP; rest-of-world GDP in current dollars at 1949 official rates was roughly 1.5-2.5x US GDP of $267B, i.e. $400-670B, at an advertising intensity of 0.4-0.8 percent (war-damaged Europe and Japan, newsprint shortages, non-commercial state broadcasting), giving $1.6-5.4B outside the US and a world total of $6.8-10.6B. (b) Top-down share: the US ran roughly 60-65 percent of world advertising when the first systematic world surveys began in the late 1960s, and its share in 1949 must have been higher because commercial broadcasting was still almost exclusively an American institution; a 60-80 percent US share puts the world total at $6.5-8.7B. Both paths overlap in the $6.5-8.7B band; central set at $7.5B with a deliberately wide interval. The IAA/Starch INRA Hooper 'Survey of World Advertising Expenditures' does not begin until the 1960s.

PRICING.summary: Broadcast pricing began as a straight rental of transmitter time. AT&T's 'toll broadcasting' station WEAF sold the Queensboro Corporation a ten-minute talk on 28 August 1922, and by 1924 AT&T was renting a basic thirteen-station network at $2,600 an hour. The networks turned that into a full rate-card business modelled on print. Every station carried a published evening-hour rate - CBS's ran from $125 to $1,250 per converted hour in 1940 - and every other daypart was a fixed fraction of it: a daytime hour cost half an evening hour, a Sunday afternoon hour two thirds or three quarters, an hour after midnight a third. Volume earned discounts from 2.5 percent up to 25 percent for advertisers billing $1.2 million a year, and NBC computed those discounts across Red and Blue together, which is exactly what the FCC seized on to prove the two networks were one business. On top of the card sat the era's intermediary stack: the agency's 15 percent, the network's retained share of net time sales, and the affiliate's compensation, which NBC paid on a step formula - the first sixteen unit hours free, then 20, 30 and 37.5 percent of the average unit rate. Mutual, which had no rate card at all, took 3.5 percent from its member stations' network proceeds. What made sponsorship different from later spot pricing is that the rate card priced only the airtime. The sponsor separately bought the show - star, writers, orchestra, announcer - and that program cost was a large minority of the total outlay. Then the war changed the arithmetic entirely: with a 90 percent excess-profits tax and a deductible institutional ad, a dollar of advertising cost a profitable corporation about fifteen cents.

MEASUREMENT.summary: Broadcasting had no circulation to audit, so the era had to invent one, and the whole history turns on who paid the counter. The Cooperative Analysis of Broadcasting began field work in March 1930 with the Association of National Advertisers' endorsement, funded by advertisers at $70 a month, and deliberately excluded the networks as subscribers until 1937 - buyers were counting the sellers' goods. Its method was 24-hour telephone recall, and its central defect was the telephone itself: by 1934-35, 96 percent of telephone subscribers owned radios but only 31 percent of American families had telephones, so the sample over-represented the well-off. Competition arrived from an unexpected funder. Clark-Hooper launched the coincidental call ('Were you listening to the radio just now?') in sixteen cities in autumn 1934, financed by magazine publishers who believed the CAB was overstating radio's audience - a rival medium bought the audit. Hooper's numbers nonetheless ran about 20 percent above the CAB's, and when McCann-Erickson's Hans Zeisel traced the gap to ring counts and busy-signal handling, and Marion Harper Jr. presented it in February 1946, the industry's own cooperative collapsed; Hooper absorbed its accounts that July. Nielsen meanwhile industrialised the count with the Audimeter, bought from its MIT inventors in 1936, piloted in Chicago from 1938, commercial from December 1942 with 800 metered homes, and projectable to 97 percent of US homes by April 1949. By then ratings were literally contract terms: Bing Crosby's right to pre-record depended on holding a 12, and CBS bought Jack Benny by guaranteeing his sponsor $3,000 a week for every Hooper point he lost. Print measurement, by contrast, was mature - the Audit Bureau of Circulations dated from 1914 - and the era's most famous complaint about advertising waste, the Wanamaker line, first appears in print in 1919 with no primary source behind it.

TARGETING.summary: Targeting in this era was a matter of time slots, maps and mailing lists - never individuals, except in the mail. The sharpest instrument was the daypart. Because a daytime network hour cost exactly half an evening hour, and because the daytime audience was overwhelmingly women at home, an advertiser who wanted homemakers bought mornings and afternoons and got them at half price. That single price rule created the daytime serial: Procter & Gamble and its agencies built the soap opera to occupy cheap hours in front of the people who bought soap. The second instrument was geography. National spot radio, bought station by station through representative firms, grew from $15 million in 1935 to $123 million in 1949, and local spot from $35 million to $245 million - by the end of the era more radio money went to local spot than to the networks. The third was editorial context: Coen's magazine split shows women's magazines taking 39 percent of all magazine advertising in 1935, and business papers and farm publications sold occupational audiences directly. The fourth, and the only one that reached a named human being, was direct mail, which carried the whole accountability tradition of keyed coupons and split-tested copy that Claude Hopkins had codified in Scientific Advertising in 1923. Measurement set the ceiling on all of it. The CAB reported audience by socioeconomic group from 1933 and split the listening day into finer and finer pieces - one recall call, then four dayparts in 1935, eight in 1940, and 32 overlapping interview sets a day by 1942 - but the finest unit anyone could actually price was a daypart in a market for a class of household. Nothing narrower was purchasable, because nothing narrower was countable.

events.title: WEAF sells the first block of broadcast time
events.desc: AT&T's 'toll broadcasting' station in New York sold the Queensboro Corporation a ten-minute talk promoting Hawthorne Court apartments in Jackson Heights. AT&T's theory was that a broadcaster should rent airtime the way the telephone company rented a circuit - the seller supplies the pipe, the buyer supplies the message. That theory, not the advertisement itself, is what era 2 is built on. Price is recorded at claim e2-pricing-001; sources conflict between $50 for ten minutes and $100 for fifteen.

events.title: NBC is formed and RCA buys AT&T out of broadcasting
events.desc: The National Broadcasting Company was incorporated with RCA holding 50 percent, General Electric 30 percent and Westinghouse 20 percent; that November RCA bought AT&T's Broadcasting Co. of America, including WEAF, for $1,000,000. AT&T left broadcasting and kept the wires. CBS followed in 1927 and Mutual in 1934, and the two-network structure that the FCC would attack in 1941 was set.

claim.statement: RCA paid $1,000,000 for AT&T's Broadcasting Co. of America, including station WEAF, in November 1926.
claim.unit: US$ millions paid by RCA for AT&T's Broadcasting Co. of America

sources.name: FCC, Report on Chain Broadcasting (May 1941), ch. I

events.title: The Cooperative Analysis of Broadcasting starts counting listeners
events.desc: After a meeting at the Yale Club on 7 February 1930, Archibald Crossley began the first continuous national audience survey with the Association of National Advertisers' endorsement but at his own financial risk. Twelve months of telephone recall interviews across 50 cities gave advertisers, for the first time, a number to put against a program. Broadcasting became priceable the moment it became countable.

claim.statement: The CAB's first-year design covered 17,000 radio families per report across 50 cities, in three four-month reports.
claim.unit: radio families covered per CAB report in its first year

sources.name: Beville, Audience Ratings: Radio, Television, Cable (1988), ch. 1

events.title: Magazine publishers pay for a rival radio rating
events.desc: Clark-Hooper launched the telephone coincidental method in sixteen cities, funded by a group of magazine publishers led by McCall's promotion director Don Parsons, who believed the advertiser-funded CAB was inflating radio's audience. The first coincidental ratings did come in lower. The episode is the cleanest demonstration in the whole history that the funder of a measurement shapes the number it produces.

events.title: The Wheeler-Lea Act gives the FTC power over deceptive advertising
events.desc: The amendment to Section 5 of the FTC Act extended the Commission's reach from 'unfair methods of competition' to 'unfair or deceptive acts or practices', gave it jurisdiction over false food, drug, device and cosmetic advertising, and let it issue cease-and-desist orders and penalties rather than merely hold hearings. Combined with the Printers' Ink model statute of 1911, it completed the private-plus-federal governance layer that US advertising carried for the rest of the century.

events.title: The FCC's Report on Chain Broadcasting exposes the network economy
events.desc: The Commission published audited financials for the whole industry and found that two companies handled more than half the business, kept nearly three quarters of network time-sales proceeds, and locked affiliates in with exclusive contracts and open-ended time options. The chain-broadcasting rules that followed forced RCA to divest one of its two networks.

claim.statement: Stations affiliated with NBC or CBS held about 92 percent of the nighttime wattage of US unlimited-time stations at the end of 1938 - about 90 percent of all US nighttime wattage. The FCC's own published summary said only 'over 85 percent'.
claim.unit: percent of US unlimited-time stations' nighttime wattage held by stations affiliated with NBC or CBS, end of 1938

sources.name: FCC, Report on Chain Broadcasting (May 1941), ch. VI - full text retrieved and searched

claim.method: From the FCC ch. VI wattage table. Stations affiliated with NBC or CBS, including dual NBC/Mutual and CBS/Mutual affiliates: 959,950 + 658,050 + 82,800 + 11,200 = 1,712,000 of 1,869,400 = 91.58 percent. Excluding the dual affiliates (NBC only + CBS only) gives 1,618,000 = 86.55 percent - the reading the FCC may have used, since it published 'over 85 percent'. The denominator is the nighttime power of the 475 unlimited-time stations, which the FCC states is 97.9 percent of the national total; against all US nighttime wattage the two readings are 89.7 and 84.7 percent. Interval floor set at 84.7 (narrow reading, national denominator) and ceiling at 91.58 (broad reading, unlimited-time denominator). Grade C rather than A because the number requires a definitional choice the FCC did not publish; only 'over 85 percent' is grade A.

events.title: The Advertising Council is incorporated
events.desc: Conceived in 1941 and incorporated on 26 February 1942, the body was renamed the War Advertising Council on 25 June 1943 and worked alongside the Office of War Information on war bonds, conservation, recruitment of women into industry and the Red Cross. Advertisers and media donated the space and time; the industry bought itself a public-service justification at exactly the moment Congress was asking whether advertising should stay tax-deductible at all.

claim.statement: The Council was launched on about $100,000 raised from advertising agencies and media associations.
claim.unit: US$ raised from agencies and media associations to fund the Advertising Council at launch

events.title: The Revenue Act of 1942 makes advertising nearly free for profitable firms
events.desc: The Act replaced the graduated 35-60 percent excess-profits schedule with a flat 90 percent rate and raised the top corporate rate from 31 to 40 percent. An IRS clarification that August confirmed that war-theme, non-product goodwill advertising remained a deductible business expense. For a company in the excess-profits bracket with nothing to sell, the arithmetic was decisive: keep advertising and the Treasury pays most of it, or stop and hand the same money to the Treasury anyway. National advertising's share of all US ad dollars rose from 51.7 percent in 1935 to 61.3 percent in 1944-45.

claim.statement: For a corporation paying the wartime excess-profits tax, a dollar of deductible advertising cost roughly 20 cents after tax.
claim.unit: US$ after-tax cost to an excess-profits-tax-paying corporation of $1.00 of deductible advertising, 1943-45
claim.method: The Revenue Act of 1942 set a flat 90 percent excess-profits rate, but paired it with an overall ceiling limiting combined normal tax, surtax and excess-profits tax to 80 percent of surtax net income, and with a post-war refund credit of 10 percent of the excess-profits tax. Four cases: 90 percent with the credit ignored = 10 cents; 90 percent with the credit valued = 19 cents; at the 80 percent ceiling with the credit ignored = 20 cents; at the ceiling with the credit valued = 28 cents (the NBER marginal-rate methodology computes this case as R = .8 x .9 = .72). Most excess-profits payers sat at or near the ceiling, so the modal figure is 19-20 cents; central set at 20, interval spanning all four cases. Secondary accounts of the period ('the government might pay up to 80 percent') agree with the 20-cent figure.

sources.name: NBER, 'Calculation of Marginal Tax Rates on Corporate Income'
Encyclopedia.com, 'Excess Profits Tax'
Stole, Advertising at War: Business, Consumers, and Government in the 1940s (University of Illinois Press, 2012)

events.title: NBC Blue is sold and becomes ABC
events.desc: Forced by the FCC's chain-broadcasting rules, RCA sold the Blue Network to Edward J. Noble, the Life Savers owner who already held WMCA. He acquired the Blue name, the line leases, the New York studios, two and a half stations and roughly 60 affiliate agreements, and renamed the company the American Broadcasting Company. Antitrust, not technology, created the third network.

events.title: The industry's own rating service dies and the vendors take over
events.desc: After the Zeisel study exposed why Hooper's numbers ran 20 percent above the CAB's, a three-person committee reported in April 1946 that the CAB 'should not be continued'; three networks - by then the service's main funders - threatened to withdraw, and a deal was struck on 17 June for Hooper to take over CAB subscribers effective 31 July. Sixteen years of buyer-controlled measurement ended. Nielsen, whose meter service had been commercial since December 1942, reached 63 percent of US homes that same year and 97 percent by April 1949, and bought Hooper's national radio and television service in March 1950. Measurement passed permanently from a committee of buyers to private vendors selling to both sides.

boundary_notes: Shared with era 1 (1840s-1917): the 15 percent agency commission and the Audit Bureau of Circulations (1914) both pre-date this era and are era 1's to establish; era 2 inherits and extends them. The Coen/McCann-Erickson annual series starts in 1919 at $1,930M, so era 1 must not present an annual series before that year - benchmark points only. The 'half my advertising is wasted' line is dated here (first print citation 1919) and labelled attributed legend, not verified. Shared with era 3 (1950-1975): era 2 hands over 1949 totals of $5,210M in US advertising, 1.9 percent of GDP, split newspapers $1,911M (36.7 percent), direct mail $756M (14.5 percent), radio $571M (11.0 percent), magazines $458M (8.8 percent), television $58M (1.1 percent), business papers $248M, billboards $131M, farm publications $55M, miscellaneous $1,022M; national $2,990M and local $2,220M. Radio's peak share of US advertising was 14.9 percent in 1945 and it was never the leading medium in any year - newspapers led in every year of this era and, per the pre-cleared constraint, out-earned television deep into later decades. Sponsorship is alive at the boundary: in 1949 the advertiser still owns the show and the network still sells only time; era 3 owns the death of that model. Two measurement facts cross the boundary: the Nielsen Radio Index reached 97 percent US coverage in April 1949, and Nielsen bought C.E. Hooper's national radio and television ratings service in March 1950 for a reported $500,000-$750,000, which is era 3's to record. For the ad/GDP thread in eras 6-7: the maximum of the entire 1919-2007 Coen/BEA series is 3.0 percent in 1922, well above the 2.5 percent reached in 2000 - the 'capture' argument must be stated against that benchmark. For the dataset layer in R2: classified is not separately reported before 1950 (first hard split, HSUS De523-526, is 1950 at $377M of $2,070M newspaper), Yellow Pages is not a separate Coen category before 1980, national/local splits begin in 1935, medium splits begin in 1935 (radio from 1926, newspapers from 1919), and the 1920s totals were revised down about 15 percent. Coen's 1938 radio figure runs about 1.66 times the FCC's audited industry net time sales for the same year, a documented seam at the very start of the signature chart. (R3 verdict application) Claim e2-creators-001 - 'JWT produced at least five of each year's top ten network radio programs' - was REJECTED in adversarial verification: neither cited source carries the statistic and no independent source for it was findable. It is replaced at the same id by the sourced 'nine weekly shows sponsored by JWT clients in 1933' datum, and the CREATORS summary's 'at least half the top ten' phrasing was rewritten to match. Any top-ten framing must be rebuilt from Crossley/CAB season rankings against agency-of-record attributions; that primary work has not been done.
